title: The Creator Guide to Leaving Instagram for a Platform You Own (2026)
html:
Instagram has a problem the other platforms do not: after more than a decade, there is still no dependable way to be paid by Instagram for making things on Instagram.

TikTok has Creator Rewards. YouTube has the Partner Programme. Instagram has had a series of bonus schemes that were invitation-only, region-limited, and then quietly discontinued — the Reels Play bonus among them. What remains for almost everybody is brand deals and affiliate links, which means the platform provides the audience and takes none of the risk while you do the selling.

This is the Instagram-specific companion to our guides on leaving TikTok and leaving YouTube.

The Instagram-specific problems

No native payout worth planning around

Bonus programmes have come and gone, never available in most countries, never guaranteed month to month, and never something a sensible person builds an income on. If you are full-time on Instagram, your actual employer is whichever brand emailed you last — and that relationship ends the moment your engagement dips.

Reach you are asked to buy back

Organic reach on a follower base you built is throttled, and the remedy on offer is promotion. You grow an audience, the platform limits how much of that audience sees you, and then sells you access to the people who already chose to follow you. Nothing about that arrangement gets better as you get bigger.

Links are treated as leakage

External links are structurally disadvantaged: one clickable link in the bio for most accounts, story links gated behind eligibility for years, and posts that point off-platform reliably under-performing. The one mechanism you need to build an audience you own is the one the platform is least willing to let you use.

The account is not yours

Follower counts are rows in Meta's database. Accounts are lost to hacks, to automated impersonation flags, and to appeal processes that route through a form and never a person. Creators with six figures of following have lost everything overnight with no recourse, and there is no export to fall back on.

Everything is a copy of something else

Reels exist because TikTok did. The product direction is set by whatever competitor is winning, which means the format you invested in learning can be deprioritised in a quarter without warning.

What owning it instead looks like

On DeHub, the decentralised social network, an upload is minted on-chain to your wallet at the moment you post. That record exists whether or not the platform does. The feed is chronological and transparent, so reach is not a lever someone can sell back to you, and the code is open-source, so the rules cannot change under you in private.

A revenue share, at all

The comparison here is not "90% versus 55%". For most Instagram creators the comparison is a published revenue share versus nothing. DeHub commits up to 90% of ad revenue back to the ecosystem and its creators, with no invitation, no region lock, and no five-figure follower gate.

Getting paid for attention directly

DeHub's watch-to-earn bounties let you attach rewards that pay viewers in crypto for genuinely watching your work. For a creator whose entire income currently depends on convincing a brand that impressions are worth something, being able to convert attention into payment without a sponsor in the middle is the whole point. Our pillar on what watch-to-earn is covers the mechanics.

Subscriptions that are assets

DeHub subscriptions are minted on-chain and are tradable, and the creator earns a royalty when one is resold — see tokenised subscriptions explained. Against Instagram, where the closest equivalent is a broadcast channel with no payment rail attached, this is a category difference rather than a feature difference.

Per-post monetisation, including for images

Every upload can be free, pay-per-view, or token-gated, and that applies to image posts and carousels, not only video. Photographers, illustrators and designers — the people Instagram was originally for and has monetised least — get a per-piece business model rather than a portfolio that earns only when somebody hires them off it.

Earnings settle in DHB, primarily on Base, an Ethereum Layer 2, with contracts on BNB Chain and Polygon. It trades on decentralised exchanges and on Coinbase and is listed on CoinGecko and CoinMarketCap.

How to migrate without torching your reach

  1. Claim your handle. Free, first-come, and worth doing today rather than the day you need it.
  2. Mirror the grid. Your existing images and Reels populate a new home in an afternoon, and they are already made.
  3. Put the archive somewhere it earns. Outtakes, full shoots, the unedited set, the process video — the material that never justified a grid slot is exactly what a per-post paywall is for.
  4. Work around the link problem deliberately. Bio link, story mentions, and on-image text, because the platform will not help you here and pretending otherwise wastes months.
  5. Turn the money on first. Set up subscriptions and revenue share before you start pointing people over, so the first arrivals land on something that works.

Instagram remains an excellent shop window. It is a terrible shop.

Frequently asked questions

Does Instagram pay creators in 2026?

Not reliably, and not everywhere. Bonus programmes such as Reels Play have been invitation-only, limited to particular countries, and discontinued. The realistic income routes on Instagram remain brand partnerships, affiliate links and selling your own product, all of which you arrange yourself.

What is the best Instagram alternative for creators?

If you want the same photo-and-Reels experience elsewhere, the alternatives keep the same arrangement. If you want a published revenue share and uploads recorded to your wallet, that is a structurally different platform — which is the category DeHub is in.

Can photographers monetise on DeHub, or is it video-first?

Image posts and carousels get the same monetisation options as video: free, pay-per-view, or token-gated, set per upload. For a photographer that means a single archive can carry free work for reach and paid work for income at the same time.

Will cross-posting hurt my Instagram reach?

Posts pointing at an external link tend to under-perform, which is a reason to be deliberate about where you place the pointer, not a reason to avoid building elsewhere. Keep posting natively on Instagram and drive traffic through the bio, stories and on-image mentions.

What happens to my content if the platform goes away?

Uploads are minted on-chain to your wallet, so the ownership record does not depend on the platform continuing to exist. That is the difference between owning your work and renting somewhere to keep it.
